entry.title: Combined summary - Silent Payments coinbase
entry.summary: Silent Payments in coinbase transactions present a significant shift toward privacy-centric payouts for cryptocurrency mining, specifically through the SPc mechanism. This protocol is rooted in BIP352 and employs static public addresses built from scan and spend keys, ensuring that miners’ payment histories remain confidential even when interacting with pools. Miners submit their Silent Payment addresses over Stratum v2, enabling pools to record and credit their hashrate without exposing sensitive transaction information. Security practices become paramount as these addresses are stored; mining pools must implement rigorous data management routines, including systematic deletion of share accounting logs after their utility lapses, drawing parallels with best practices observed by VPN providers. The technical integration of Silent Payments into the coinbase process introduces unique cryptographic challenges due to the structure of coinbase transactions, which lack traditional inputs. SPc counters this by deriving a nonce from the block height and a pool-specific public key, thereby protecting against attacks outlined in BIP352. The miner’s public key (`A_send`) replaces conventional identifiers within the coinbase script, facilitating necessary cryptographic operations for payment determination. Adoption of SPc necessitates adaptations in payout computation and may require mining pools to revise structures for accommodating smaller payments, perhaps referencing solutions like Ocean’s use of BOLT12 Lightning Network payments. Constraints on the number of outputs per coinbase transaction also demand careful handling to avoid dust outputs and manage payout scalability. Widespread adoption and evolution of SPc rely heavily on community engagement via platforms such as [GitHub](https://github.com/average-gary/silent-pool), where test vectors and developmental resources are available. This collaborative approach not only fosters specification refinement but also paves the way for formal recognition as a Bitcoin Improvement Proposal (BIP). As SPc matures, it brings forth new operational complexities and security considerations that must be thoughtfully addressed to ensure miner privacy while maintaining robust mining processes. Compatibility with existing digital wallets remains an essential concern. It is imperative to clarify whether current wallet software can recognize and process Silent Payments or if updates are required. A dedicated compatibility section becomes invaluable, outlining prerequisites that allow both users and miners to prepare adequately before adopting SPc-based transactions. Detailed documentation on compatibility ensures seamless integration and minimizes unforeseen issues during transition to Silent Payments. Technical discussion surrounding BIP34 highlights the implications of block height encoding for coinbase scriptSig construction. With block heights currently between 65,536 and 16,777,216, encoding consumes four bytes—one for push length and three for data—with possible expansion to five bytes as heights increase. This affects the available space for extranonce allocation. After accounting for a typical 34-byte `A_send`, approximately 62 bytes are left for the extranonce. While sufficient at present, future growth in block height will further constrain this space, underscoring the need for efficient encoding strategies. Wallets require tailored scanning profiles due to the nonstandard placement of ownership-identifying data in SPc transactions, differing from standard Silent Payments. Specialized protocols are needed to securely and efficiently identify ownership, ensuring that wallet operations remain precise and robust even as data management requirements diverge from established patterns. Concerns about extranonce constraints related to increasing block heights appear mitigated by advancements such as [BIP323](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/2a783793f45d81558c2cecc7749f94226660ed54/bip-0323.mediawiki). BIP323 outlines scalable solutions for managing larger data requirements as blockchain technology evolves, maintaining efficiency and obviating drastic architectural changes. Recent developments have allowed approximately 2% of miners, notably through Ocean, to receive direct coinbase payouts instead of relying solely on custodial pools. In this system, miners can build blocks independently using Datum, with payouts linked to unique Bitcoin addresses. However, this methodology exposes privacy risks, including address reuse and increased traceability. Implementing Silent Payments would decouple future payouts from identifiable addresses, improving privacy for miners. Adopting this system would primarily affect transaction-receiving entities—wallets, libraries, and scanners—while specialized mining software would handle sending. Whether SPc can be integrated into BIP-352 or requires a distinct proposal remains under discussion, especially for solo pools where individualized requirements may arise. Nevertheless, the privacy gains from obscuring block reward spending details make SPc a compelling option, provided implementation is sensitive to current solo mining practices. The dual-payout scheme introduced by SPc divides payouts based on size: larger amounts are paid on-chain via direct coinbase outputs, while smaller sums are accumulated off-chain and dispatched to an Ark user pubkey (`U`). Distinct cryptographic tweaks derived from ECDH per transaction preserve privacy and data independence across payout tiers. On-chain transactions employ serialized ECDH keys and domain-separated tweaks, whereas off-chain transactions utilize blinded mailbox identifiers to secure funds transfer without disrupting Ark server setups.
